analogy.p: Imagine electrons as a crowd walking through a room full of people standing still (the ions). When the room is quiet and the people stand still, the crowd gets through easily. When the standing people start to wobble and sway more (the ions vibrating as the lamp heats up), the crowd bumps into them far more often and finds it harder to get through, so the resistance goes up. The analogy breaks down because the standing people do not stop the walkers from carrying energy, and in a real wire the electrons keep drifting in one direction because of the electric field, whereas a crowd has no field pushing it.
analogy.t: A crowd walking through a room

bullets: **Independent variable**: the potential difference across the component, in volts (V), changed using the variable resistor.
**Dependent variable**: the current through the component, in amps (A), read from the ammeter.
The **resistance** is never measured directly; it is calculated from **R = V / I** (or found from the shape of the graph).
Each component gives a different shaped graph because each behaves differently as current and temperature change.
Three components, three graphs: straight line (resistor), S-shaped curve (lamp), one-way curve (diode).
The **I-V characteristic** is the graph of current (y-axis) against potential difference (x-axis).
Key idea to say: the **shape** of the graph tells you whether resistance is constant or changing.
core.p: The required practical asks you to **use circuit diagrams to set up and check appropriate circuits** to investigate the **I-V characteristics** of three components: a **fixed resistor at constant temperature**, a **filament lamp** and a **diode**. An I-V characteristic is a graph that shows how the **current (I)** through a component changes as the **potential difference (V)** across it changes. Because current and p.d. are the only things you measure, the practical also tests how well you can control variables, choose ranges and interpret the shape of a graph. You then use the shapes to say how the **resistance** of each component behaves.

bullets: **Ammeter in series** with the component: it has a very **low resistance**, so it does not change the current it measures.
**Voltmeter in parallel** across the component only (not across the cell and not across the ammeter): it has a very **high resistance**, so almost no current is diverted through it.
**Variable resistor in series**: changing its resistance changes the current, and so changes the p.d. across the test component.
**Switch** (or disconnect a wire) so that the circuit can be turned off between readings.
**Cell or d.c. supply**: provides the p.d.; reversing its connections gives negative values.

Use correct **circuit symbols**: cell, switch, ammeter (circle with A), voltmeter (circle with V), variable resistor (rectangle with an arrow through it), resistor (rectangle), filament lamp (circle with a cross), diode (triangle with a bar).
A diagram with the voltmeter in series, or the ammeter in parallel, will score no marks for the circuit.
core.h: The circuit and why every part is there
core.p: The circuit is a **series loop** containing a **cell (or variable d.c. power supply)**, a **variable resistor**, an **ammeter** and the **test component**. The **voltmeter** is then connected **in parallel** across the test component only. The ammeter must be in series because it measures the current, which is the same at every point of a series loop. The voltmeter must be in parallel because it measures the difference in energy per unit charge between two points, so it must be connected across the two ends of the component. Marks are regularly lost by putting the voltmeter in the wrong place or drawing the wrong symbol.

bullets: **1.** Connect the cell, switch, ammeter, variable resistor and the component in series.
**2.** Connect the voltmeter in parallel across the component.
**3.** Set the variable resistor to its largest resistance (smallest current) and close the switch.
**4.** Read and record the p.d. from the voltmeter and the current from the ammeter in a results table.
**5.** Open the switch (or disconnect) so the component cools back down.
**6.** Move the variable resistor to reduce its resistance, close the switch and record a new pair of readings.
**7.** Repeat for **at least six** different p.d. values, spread evenly up to the maximum safe value for the component.
**8.** Repeat the whole method for the other two components, keeping the same layout.
core.p: The method is the same for all three components, so it is worth learning once and then changing only the component. You build the circuit, set a low p.d. and record the current and p.d., then change the variable resistor to alter the p.d. and repeat. The key skill is to take **enough readings across a suitable range** so that the graph shape is clear, and to **switch the circuit off between readings** so the component does not warm up and change its resistance unfairly (especially important for the fixed resistor).

bullets: Reverse the cell, **not** the meters, unless the meters would otherwise read backwards (then swap the meter leads too).
The negative readings are plotted as **negative p.d. (left of the origin)** and **negative current (below the origin)**.
For the fixed resistor and the lamp the third-quadrant graph is a mirror image rotated through 180 degrees: the shape is the same in both directions.
For the **diode** the reverse readings show **almost zero current**, even at large negative p.d.
A diode needs a **protective resistor** in series to stop the forward current becoming large enough to damage it.
Use a **milliammeter** (smaller range) to read the very small currents of the diode accurately.
Remember to record the sign of every reading in the table.
core.h: Reversing the connections to get negative values
core.p: An I-V characteristic covers both directions of current, so you need readings with the **current flowing the other way**. To do this you **reverse the connections to the cell** (swap the two wires at the cell or turn the power supply polarity), which reverses the direction of the current and gives **negative p.d. and negative current readings**. You then repeat the method. The two sets of readings are plotted on one graph with positive values in the first quadrant and negative values in the third quadrant. For the diode this is essential because the whole point is to show what happens in the **reverse direction**.

bullets: **Shape**: straight line through the origin, in both quadrants.
**Meaning**: I is directly proportional to V, so **resistance is constant**.
**Gradient of an I-V graph = 1 / R**, so a **steeper line means a lower resistance**.
The line only stays straight if the **temperature stays constant**; this is why you switch off between readings.
An ohmic conductor obeys **Ohm's law**: p.d. across it is directly proportional to current, at constant temperature.
If you plot V against I instead, the gradient equals R.
A resistor with a larger resistance gives a **shallower** I-V line than one with a smaller resistance.
core.p: For a **fixed resistor kept at a constant temperature** the I-V characteristic is a **straight line through the origin**. This means the current is **directly proportional** to the p.d.: doubling the p.d. doubles the current. The resistance, found from R = V / I, is therefore the **same at every point** on the line. A component that behaves like this is called an **ohmic conductor**. The reason resistance is constant is that, at constant temperature, the **ions in the metal vibrate by the same amount**, so electrons collide with them at the same rate whatever the current.

bullets: **Shape**: S-shaped through the origin (steeper near 0 V, flatter at high positive and negative p.d.).
**Resistance increases as temperature increases**: the lamp is a **non-ohmic conductor**.
The energy transferred by electrons colliding with ions heats the filament (the **heating effect of a current**).
At high temperature the lamp gives out light because the filament becomes white hot.
The **graph is symmetrical**: the same shape happens for current in the reverse direction.
Calculate R = V / I at any point to see that R is larger at higher p.d.
Do **not** use the gradient to find resistance on a curve: take V and I at the point and divide.
core.p: For a **filament lamp** the I-V characteristic is a **curve that gets shallower as the p.d. increases**, passing through the origin. The line bends towards the V-axis, so the **gradient decreases**, which means the **resistance increases** as the current increases. The explanation is about temperature: as the current increases, the **filament gets hotter**. A hotter filament means the **ions in the metal wire vibrate more**, so the **electrons collide with the ions more frequently**. More collisions mean more opposition to the flow of charge, so the **resistance increases**, and the current rises by less for each extra volt.

bullets: **Forward direction**: low resistance once above the threshold; current rises steeply.
**Reverse direction**: **very high resistance**, so effectively no current flows.
A diode is therefore used to make sure current flows in only one direction, for example to convert a.c. to d.c. (rectification).
Always use a **protective resistor** in series, otherwise the large forward current can burn out the diode.
A **light-emitting diode (LED)** is a diode that emits light when current flows in the forward direction.
A diode is a **non-ohmic** component: the graph is not a straight line.
Use the milliamp range of the ammeter: forward currents are small and reverse currents are tiny.
core.p: A **diode** allows current to flow in **one direction only**. Its I-V characteristic shows that in the **forward direction** the current is **almost zero until the p.d. reaches a threshold of roughly 0.6 to 0.7 V** for a silicon diode, then it **increases very rapidly** for a small further increase in p.d. In the **reverse direction** the current is **almost zero** whatever the p.d. (up to the breakdown voltage), which means the diode has a **very high resistance** in the reverse direction. The resistance of a diode therefore **depends on the direction of the p.d.** and also falls steeply once it is conducting.

bullets: **Straight line through the origin**: resistance constant (ohmic conductor).
**Curve getting shallower**: resistance increasing (filament lamp).
**Zero current then sudden steep rise**: diode conducting above a threshold.
To find resistance at a point, read V and I from the graph and use **R = V / I**.
Plot the **independent variable (V) on the x-axis** and the dependent variable (I) on the y-axis.
Use a **sensible scale** that makes the plotted points fill more than half of the grid.
Draw the line or curve of best fit freehand for the lamp and diode; use a ruler only for the resistor.
Circle and ignore any **anomalous result**, but mention that it could be repeated.
core.p: In an exam you may be asked to **sketch**, **label**, **identify** or **interpret** an I-V graph. Always put **current on the y-axis** and **potential difference on the x-axis**, label both axes with units, draw the axes crossing at the origin so negative values show, and draw a **smooth line or curve of best fit** through the points. To interpret the graph, think about how the **gradient** changes: for I against V the gradient equals 1 / R, so a gradient that decreases means resistance increases, and a gradient that increases means resistance decreases.

bullets: **Switch off between readings** so the component does not heat up and change resistance (especially the resistor).
Use the **same component, same wires and same meters** throughout each run.
Take **at least six readings** across the range so the shape is clear.
Check each meter for a **zero error** before starting.
**Repeat** the readings, calculate a mean for each p.d. and plot the mean values to improve reliability.
Choose **meter ranges** that give a reading over most of the scale (use mA range for the diode).
A fault such as a loose connection can give an **anomalous** point, which should be identified and repeated.
core.p: A fair investigation changes only the p.d. and measures the current, so everything else that affects resistance must be controlled. The most important is **temperature**, which changes the resistance of the lamp (deliberately, as part of what is being shown) and which would change the resistance of the fixed resistor if the current were left on for too long. To make results **more reliable** you repeat readings and calculate a mean; to make them **more accurate** you use suitable meter ranges and read the scale carefully at eye level, avoiding zero errors.

bullets: **Hot filament lamp or wires**: risk of burns; control by switching off between readings and letting components cool before touching them.
**Overheating resistor**: control by keeping the current small and only closing the switch briefly.
**Damage to the diode** by a large forward current: control by using a protective resistor in series.
**Short circuit**: check the circuit before switching on; do not connect the supply directly across the ammeter.
Keep water and liquids away from the electrical equipment.
Do not use a supply with a p.d. higher than needed for the component rating.
Check that wires are not damaged or frayed before connecting them.
core.p: The practical uses low voltages, so the main risks are not electric shock but **heat** and **damage to components**. The wires and the resistor can become hot if a large current flows for a long time, and a filament lamp becomes very hot, so a student could be burned. A diode that is not protected can overheat. A good risk assessment names a hazard, the harm it causes and a sensible control measure.

bullets: **R = V / I** (resistance in ohms = potential difference in volts divided by current in amps).
**Power P = I x V = I squared x R** explains why the lamp heats up: higher current means more energy transferred per second.
**Thermistor** (NTC): resistance **decreases** as temperature increases, so its graph curves the opposite way to the lamp.
**LDR**: resistance **decreases** as light intensity increases.
The resistance of a **metal wire** increases with length because the electrons collide with more ions (see the wire-length practical).
The idea of an **ohmic conductor** links to Ohm's law and to why most metals at constant temperature give straight I-V lines.
In exam questions, the phrase **'at constant temperature'** is a clue that the answer should be a straight line.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier ideas
core.p: This practical links the idea of **resistance** to the behaviour of real components and brings together several equations. It connects directly to **charge flow, current and p.d.**, to **R = V / I**, to the **heating effect** of a current (**P = I squared R**) and to the sensor components, the **thermistor** and the **LDR**, which also have non-straight I-V characteristics. In Higher-tier questions you may be asked to use values read from the graph to calculate resistance at different points and to give a full explanation in terms of electrons colliding with vibrating ions.

exam: **Describe** questions (usually 4 to 6 marks): give the circuit with ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel, say how you change the p.d. with a variable resistor, how many readings, and that you reverse the cell for negative values.
**Draw a circuit diagram** (2 to 3 marks): correct symbols, ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel across the component, variable resistor in series, and a complete loop with no gaps.
**Sketch a graph** (2 marks): axes labelled I (y) and V (x), correct shape, passing through the origin, and showing both quadrants if asked.
**Explain** the lamp (3 marks): current increases, so temperature of the filament increases; ions vibrate more; more frequent collisions with electrons, so resistance increases.
**Explain the resistor** (2 marks): straight line through the origin means current is directly proportional to p.d., so resistance is constant at constant temperature.
**Diode** questions (2 to 3 marks): current flows in one direction only; very high resistance in the reverse direction; threshold voltage before it conducts.
**Calculate** with R = V / I (2 marks): write the equation, substitute with units and give the answer with its unit (ohms).
**Control variables** (1 to 2 marks): switch off between readings so temperature stays constant; use the same component.
**Risk** questions (2 marks): name the hazard (hot lamp or wire), the harm (burns) and a control (switch off, allow to cool).
**Evaluate or improve** (2 marks): take more readings, repeat and average, use a smaller step at the threshold of a diode.
Always use the phrase **'at constant temperature'** when describing the resistor's straight-line graph.

mistakes.r: The filament gets hotter, so the ions vibrate more and there are more frequent collisions between electrons and ions, increasing resistance.
mistakes.w: The lamp's resistance increases because the current is bigger, so there are more electrons.

mistakes.r: The voltmeter must be connected in parallel across the component only; the ammeter is the one in series.
mistakes.w: Putting the voltmeter in series with the component.

mistakes.r: It is a straight line through the origin only at constant temperature.
mistakes.w: Saying the resistor's graph is straight with no condition.

mistakes.r: It has a low resistance in the forward direction once the threshold p.d. is exceeded and a very high resistance in reverse.
mistakes.w: Saying the diode has no resistance in the forward direction.

mistakes.r: On an I-V graph the gradient is 1 / R for a straight line only; for a curve use R = V / I at the point.
mistakes.w: Using the gradient of the I-V curve as the resistance.

mistakes.r: For an I-V characteristic plot current on the y-axis against potential difference on the x-axis.
mistakes.w: Plotting V on the y-axis and I on the x-axis.

mistakes.r: The lamp curve gets shallower (gradient decreases) as p.d. increases because resistance increases.
mistakes.w: Drawing a lamp graph as a straight line or a curve that gets steeper.

mistakes.r: A steeper I-V line means a lower resistance because the gradient equals 1 / R.
mistakes.w: Saying a steeper I-V graph means a higher resistance.

mistakes.r: A protective resistor limits the forward current so the diode is not damaged.
mistakes.w: Not mentioning the protective resistor for a diode.

summary: You must be able to describe and carry out the required practical that investigates the current-potential difference (I-V) characteristics of a fixed resistor at constant temperature, a filament lamp and a diode, drawing the circuit, taking positive and negative readings and sketching and explaining each graph. It matters because the practical, its graph shapes and the explanations (especially why a lamp's resistance rises) are tested in almost every Paper 1 series.

terms.d: A graph of current through a component against the potential difference across it.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit, measured in volts.
The rate of flow of electric charge, measured in amps.
The opposition to the flow of charge in a component, found from R = V / I and measured in ohms.
A conductor whose current is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, at constant temperature, giving a straight line I-V graph through the origin.
A component whose I-V graph is not a straight line through the origin, so its resistance changes with current or p.d.
A lamp containing a thin metal wire that gets hot when current flows, and whose resistance increases as its temperature increases.
A component that has very high resistance in one direction and low resistance in the other, so that current flows in one direction only.
The forward p.d. at which a diode starts to conduct, about 0.6 to 0.7 V for silicon.
A resistor whose resistance can be changed, used to change the current and p.d. in a circuit.
A meter with very low resistance connected in series to measure current.
A meter with very high resistance connected in parallel to measure potential difference.
The transfer of energy to thermal energy stores when charge carriers collide with ions in a conductor.
A resistor in series with a diode to limit the current and prevent damage to the diode.
A variable that is kept the same so that only the independent variable affects the dependent variable.
A reading that does not fit the pattern of the other results and should be checked or repeated.

worked.ans: R = 5.0 ohms, 7.5 ohms and 10 ohms. Resistance increases because the higher current heats the filament, so the ions vibrate more and collide more frequently with the electrons.
worked.q: A student measures the p.d. across and the current through a filament lamp. At 2.0 V the current is 0.40 A, at 6.0 V it is 0.80 A and at 12.0 V it is 1.2 A. Calculate the resistance at each p.d. and explain the trend. (5 marks)
steps: The resistance increases as the p.d. and current increase.
The filament gets hotter, so the ions vibrate more and electrons collide with them more often.

worked.ans: Resistance = 20 ohms; current at 9.0 V = 0.45 A.
worked.q: The I-V graph for a fixed resistor at constant temperature passes through the origin and through the point (6.0 V, 0.30 A). Calculate the resistance and the current at 9.0 V. (4 marks)
steps: The graph is a straight line through the origin, so the resistor is ohmic and R is constant.
Check: the current is directly proportional to p.d. (9.0 / 6.0 = 1.5, and 0.30 x 1.5 = 0.45 A).

worked.ans: Set up a series circuit containing a cell, a switch, a variable resistor, an ammeter, a protective resistor and the diode, and connect a voltmeter in parallel across the diode only. Adjust the variable resistor to change the p.d. across the diode, and at each setting record the p.d. and the current. Take at least six readings, with smaller steps near 0.6 to 0.7 V where the current starts to rise. Reverse the connections to the cell and repeat to obtain readings in the reverse direction, where the current is almost zero. The protective resistor stops a large current damaging the diode. Plot current on the y-axis against p.d. on the x-axis and draw a smooth curve: almost no current until about 0.7 V in the forward direction, then a steep rise, and almost zero current in reverse.
worked.q: Describe how you would investigate the I-V characteristic of a diode. Include a circuit and how you would get a full set of results. (6 marks)
steps: Circuit (1 mark): cell, switch, variable resistor, ammeter and protective resistor in series with the diode; voltmeter in parallel across the diode.
Change p.d. (1 mark): adjust the variable resistor to change the p.d. across the diode.
Readings (1 mark): record p.d. and current at each setting, at least six values, smaller steps near 0.7 V.
Reverse (1 mark): reverse the cell connections to get negative p.d. and current.
Safety (1 mark): protective resistor stops a large forward current damaging the diode; switch off between readings.
Graph (1 mark): plot I against V and draw a smooth curve; describe the shape.
